subject: Chemistry
title: Spontaneous Combustion of Hay
description: A 60-second lesson on Spontaneous Combustion of Hay.

hook.text: Wet hay stored in a barn can burst into flames by itself. No spark needed.

buildup.text: Bacteria in damp hay start decomposing it. This biological process slowly releases heat.

discovery.text: If the hay is packed tight, heat can't escape. Temperature climbs past 150°C and ignition begins.

twist.text: This destroys barns worldwide every year. Farmers must dry hay below 20% moisture to prevent it.

climax.text: Spontaneous combustion is real—not supernatural. It's biology producing heat that chemistry ignites.

punchline.text: Wet hay, trapped heat, no spark. Bacteria start the fire.

quiz.question: What causes hay to spontaneously combust?
options: Bacterial decomposition generates heat that can't escape

details.summary: Wet hay can spontaneously combust because bacterial decomposition in moist conditions generates heat. If the heat cannot dissipate faster than it accumulates, temperatures rise past the ignition point of the hay, causing it to burst into flames without any external spark.
details.whyItMatters: Spontaneous hay combustion causes devastating barn fires worldwide. Understanding the chemistry of biological heat generation helps farmers store hay safely and prevents agricultural losses.
takeaways: Bacterial decomposition of moist hay generates internal heat
Insufficient ventilation allows heat to build to ignition point
Monitoring internal hay temperature prevents barn fires

faq.question: At what moisture level does hay become a spontaneous combustion risk?
faq.answer: Hay baled above twenty percent moisture content is at significant risk. Above twenty-five percent, bacterial activity accelerates rapidly. Temperatures above 150 degrees Fahrenheit inside the bale indicate immediate danger, and above 175 degrees, ignition is imminent.

faq.question: Can hay literally catch fire with no source of ignition whatsoever?
faq.answer: Yes. The bacteria generate enough heat through exothermic decomposition reactions to reach the hay's ignition temperature of approximately 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The process is entirely self-sustaining once the heat feedback loop is established.
